Experimental research accounted for 75% of the HOST Turbine Heat Transfer subproject, while analytical efforts accounted for approximately 25%.

The project covered phenomena like film-cooled airfoils, passage curvature, endwall flows, boundary layer transition, tip regions, free-stream turbulence, impingement, and turbulated serpentine passages.

The stator-airfoil heat transfer experiments showed the effects of Reynolds number, turbulence level, Mach number, temperature ratio, acceleration, and boundary layer transition on heat transfer coefficients.
The experiments on three-dimensional flow in curved passages showed the development of a vortex in the duct corner near the low pressure surface.
The real-engine environment experiments showed substantial differences between experimental airfoil temperatures and typical design system temperatures for full-coverage, film-cooled airfoils.
The high free-stream turbulence experiments showed heat transfer augmentation up to 5X at high turbulence intensities, but only 3X if the turbulence length scale was changed.
The rotor-stator interaction experiments showed a substantial impact of inlet turbulence on the first stator heat transfer, but a minimal impact on the rotor heat transfer.

The STAN5 boundary layer code required empirical coefficients to modify the free-stream turbulence intensity and gas stream enthalpy boundary conditions to predict the Stanton number reduction for showerhead film cooling.
The modified Lam-Bremhorst k-epsilon turbulence model was able to reasonably well predict the augmentation of heat transfer on the pressure surface over the fully turbulent value.
The Navier-Stokes MINT code was able to provide good heat transfer predictions compared to the Allison Gas Turbine data, but required the location of boundary layer transition to be specified.
The HOST project was a building-block approach that ranged from studying fundamental phenomena and analytical modeling to experiments in simulated real-engine environments.

The project created extensive experimental datasets depicting three-dimensional flow fields, high free-stream turbulence, boundary layer transition, film cooling effects, rough-wall cooling enhancement, and rotor-stator interaction effects.
The project aimed to move from a correlation-based approach to a more analytical-based approach for turbine heat transfer technology.
The project involved a collaboration between government, industry, and universities to advance turbine heat transfer modeling and understanding.
The project identified that existing data was insufficient to support the move to a more analytical-based approach, and increasing both the size and quality of the data was essential.
